speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: INQUIRY RESPECTING REPORTED LAY-OFF OF SHOP EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
I
should like to submit a question to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe). I have received a petition signed by a large number of employees of the Canadian National Railway
shops at Leaside, protesting against their dismissal taking place to-day. I understood from the Minister of Transport the other day that he was conferring with the railway management and the heads of the unions concerning the matter of lay-offs. I wonder if he would mind giving the house the result of that conference.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: INQUIRY RESPECTING REPORTED LAY-OFF OF SHOP EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
As a result of a conference held yesterday in my office between the railway management and a committee of the heads of the shopmen's brotherhood, it was decided that the situation would be again reviewed in the light of representations made by the management and myself as to the extreme undesirability of laying off men at this time. Following a quick telegraphic vote, it was decided that the reduction in work in the central and western regions would be taken care of by a reduction in hours; that is, instead of a twenty-four day month as the schedules now call for the men will accept an eighteen-day month, and no men will lose their employment.
In the eastern region, however, the shopmen decided that they must insist on the maintenance of the schedules; so there will be a lay-off at Moncton and at Riviere du Loup. However, I am happy to say that the business level in the maritime division is somewhat higher than on the rest of the system, therefore the lay-off will not be very extensive.
It was agreed that this condition shall stand until June 1. In May, all the railway brotherhoods are meeting in convention, and will review their position. If that meeting decides that the schedules must be maintained, that decision must be effective on June 1. On the other hand if the convention decides that the system now being followed is preferable, then that system will continue.
On my own behalf I wish to thank the brotherhoods and the shopmen themselves for taking care of this situation in such a way as not to increase unemployment. I fully realize that the senior shopmen in sacrificing their schedules have made a real sacrifice for the sake of the younger men who would otherwise be thrown out of employment. I think the spirit that has been shown is one that every one of us should commend most highly.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT

speechtext: The house resumed from Wednesday, March 30, consideration of the motion of Mr. Dunning for committee of supply, the amendment thereto of Mr. Blackmore, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Bennett.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext:
I appreciate greatly, and so do the members of our group, the tolerance, courtesy and attention which so far have been accorded to us, not only in this debate but in the previous debates in the house. We realize, no one realizes more keenly, how strange our ideas must appear to hon. members, because all we have to do is to go back four years in our own experience and remember how we felt. We can therefore tell exactly how other hon. members feel. In the light of these things we have no fault whatsoever to find with the tendency on the part of some to scoff at our notions and treat them lightly. But notwithstanding this, we contend that when the realities of the situation and the facts of our proposals are fully comprehended, there will be on all sides nothing but respect and sympathy for our contentions, whether or not it is decided in the end that they are sound.
We have been accused of wasting time. We have deliberately refrained from participating in many debates in this house. There has been very little comment by social crediters on many measures, and little or no discussion of tariff matters; not because we have not our convictions and our beliefs, but because we were deliberately refraining from speaking so that the time we felt was rightfully ours could be devoted to discussion of the matter which we believe of greater importance to this country than anything else that could be discussed at the present time.
Yesterday the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) delayed proceedings while he put on Hansard some things of which some day he and his descendants will not be so very proud.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: He has no descendants.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext:
It is too bad he has none, because I think if he had he would be a wiser man. I heard of a story concerning his province; that the first telephone to be put into the office of one of the chief men in Ontario was indignantly kicked out of the office by that man and condemned as an utterly foolhardy device with which he would have nothing to do. If the hon. member has heard that story it should give him cause for thought. The hon. gentleman I believe urged that business men should be given charge of the affairs of this country, and I should like to turn for a moment to this matter of business men managing our affairs. If hon. members will turn to the Dictionary of American Biography, volume XVII, at page 514 they will find an enlightening account of the life of a certain man named William Stanley, who lived from 1858 to 1916. Of him these words are recorded there:
He devised the multiple system of alternating current distribution, together with its equipment (patent No. 372942, issued November 8, 1887), but Westinghouse-
A business man, mark you.
-refused to finance its development until Stanley at his own expense had put the system into regular commercial service in Great Barrington, installing it in several stores.
From that invention up to the present time there have developed in the United States, I am told, businesses worth thirteen and a half billion dollars. Are business men wise? It hardly looks that way, does it? It takes more than business to make a man wise. At the same time Edison was the greatest authority on electricity in the world. Edison opposed this device as an impractical piece of nonsense. It would not work; it could not work; we did not need it. Again, Edison was a business man. Mr. Stanley's invention made possible the first alternating current transmission of electricity. From his invention came to be promoted the distribution of power by an alternating current system. It threatened the direct current system, in which Edison was deeply interested. Edison and other great authorities on electricity at that time ridiculed Stanley and opposed him by every means at their disposal. With such things as this in the records of history, Mr. Speaker, let us not be greatly surprised if even to-day new ideas meet with intolerance, misunderstanding and opposition.
While we are on the question of electricity I should like to suggest a little illustration which I believe will apply to the debate which

Use of Canada's Financial Resources
has taken place up to the present time. Before men learned to use electricity produced from the energy of a stream they had to learn by painful experience that it was possible to change into electricity the energy contained in the ice cold waters pouring down from the mountains. When they were convinced that this could be done, they were prepared to consider the possibility of erecting a plant to do that thing. After they had learned the possibility of erecting such a plant it was time to consider the possibility of distributing the electricity. After that they could occupy themselves with the matter of using the electricity when it was distributed, and of safeguarding its use. In this debate we are contending in this house that pouring down the hills of the Dominion of Canada, so to speak, there are vast torrents filled with energy which can be transformed into a form useful to mankind. There is very little value in talking about the kind of plant we should erect or how to distribute it or safeguard it until we first determine whether or not the thing can be done. In this debate we have been occupied with the question, can the thing be done? Is it possible to change vast quantities of goods and services, which are being produced and consumed in this country in one gigantic stream, into money?
Yesterday the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) offered us an Alberta bank. I must spend a moment discussing this proposal. Yesterday I issued to the press, at their request, a statement which I think it is only fair should go into Hansard:
The Canadian banking system can take a one dollar bill of the dominion or of the Bank of Canada and safely create ten dollars of cheque book money against it. This was definitely proved and acknowledged during the debate on the motion of want of confidence. In using this power, however, the banks have to go forward together in step, so to speak. This all well informed people know.
An Alberta chartered bank under the present set-up in Canada would have to get its Bank of Canada bills from the Bank of Canada, just as any other Canadian chartered bank would have to do. This fact would force the Alberta bank to conform to the policy of the Bank of Canada. Further, if such Alberta bank began to pursue any other policy it would get out of step with other Canadian chartered banks and so become in danger of losing its cash to them. This would of course render it likely to fail. An Alberta bank alone would therefore be unlikely to help in the introduction of social credit.
The Bank of Canada Act gives to the Bank of Canada the power to take one dollar of gold and create against it four dollars of Bank of Canada bills. If Mr. Dunning would offer to Alberta the poTver to give an Alberta bank this right then he would be conferring upon
Alberta real monetary power with great possibilities. If in addition lie would agree to recognize as legal tender Alberta one dollar bills with twenty-five cents of gold backing, as he does with Bank of Canada bills with twenty-five cents of gold backing, the possibilities would be still greater. The Alberta bank could then build upon one dollar of gold a currency and credit structure of $40, as the Bank of Canada with the Canadian chartered banks now can.
The power of creating legal tender bills, however, is not in his offer, I take it, and will not, I fancy, ever be in his offer.
I might add these words, which did not go out to the press: It is not the banks we are after, but the system which gives to them and to them only the creation of Canada's money. An Alberta bank attempting to establish itself to-day would probably have about as much chance of success as an Alberta distributing house would have in competition with the T. Eaton Company.
I turn now to a consideration of my motion.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext:
Would the hon. member permit a question?
Mr. BLACIvMORE: If Mr. Speaker will give me extra time I shall be glad to permit interruptions.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext:
In his statement the hon. member asked if Mr. Dunning would do so and so. In that connection I wish to say merely this, if the hon. member will permit me, that the things he there states Mr. Dunning should do are not within Mr. Dunning's power. What my hon. friend asks there is that the parliament of Canada should turn over to the social credit party the complete control of currency and credit in Canada which is now vested in this parliament, and also complete control of the Bank of Canada. I cannot do that. My hon. friend may convince parliament

if he can-but it is useless to ask me to do more than I offered to do last night, something which it was within my power to do.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: I gathered from the remarks the Minister of Finance had previously made that in him, the Minister of Finance, rested complete control of currency and credit in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext:
No, no; I repeatedly
denied any such thing, and have stated directly the opposite. In this parliament, and in the instrumentality created by this parliament, rests that power. I hope the hon. member will not repeat the statement, which has been made by several of his group, that I control

Use of Canada's Financial Resources
currency and credit in Canada. It must be within the knowledge of every hon. member of the house that I have never said that.

This is very good. In 1935, before the Bank of Canada was formed, I understand the dominion had delegated the power to create dollar bills, and credit, to each of at least eleven chartered banks throughout the country. I am going to ask this question, sir; whether or not one of the nine sovereign provinces of the dominion would be likely to mismanage currency and credit of Canada to any greater degree than would the group of men who constitute a bank. If the power lay in this parliament to give this complete power to banking institutions, before the Bank of Canada was formed, then it looks as though that power would permit giving a similar right to a province.
However, this is beside the point, although it has been an interesting sidelight. We are now discussing a motion made by the social credit group on March 8. That was a want of confidence motion, on the ground that the present government is neglecting to use Canada's resources for the abolition of poverty in the country. It is a most remarkable thing to me that, other than social crediters, hon. members who have participated in the debate have discussed anything and everything except the motion. That is a most interesting fact. Yesterday we even got to salt fish.
We had electricity this morning.

No defence has been made. I challenge members of this house to point to one single place where a defence was made by any member or supporter of the government against the charge that the government has not used the resources of the country to remove poverty. In fact, there have been no answers to any of my contentions concerning money. I directed the attention of the house and the country to money, and the point has been completely sidestepped. A red herring was dragged in, and the time of the house was spent discussing the red herring, while the money question remained in abeyance.
In a few moments I shall show that not a single contention was disproved. Let me recall to the minds of hon. members the points I made. I shall review them briefly.
First: Money is either currency or credit. It could and should be created by the king or by the state.
Second: Our money now is created by and comes from banks. This has been abundantly shown in the discussion.
Third: What gives money value is goods and services, and the producing and consuming power of the community. Had the attention of the house been directed to a discussion of that proposition the time would have been excellently spent. When the truth regarding that proposition is fully recognized we shall be on our way to a change which might do us some good.
Fourth: The amount of money that Canada can have depends upon the number of exchanges Canada can manage to bring to pass within the country. Not one word was said about that. Yet, sir, next to the other one I have mentioned, this is the most important question which can be brought to the attention of parliament.
Fifth: King-created money is sound.
Sixth: Canada's financial set-up now enables her to create legally $80 for one dollar of gold. That was established in the discussion. But before it was established the people in Alberta were called all sorts of lunatics and fools, and withstood a great amount of abuse, from a wide variety of people because that was our contention. It is established, sir, and a great achievement has been brought to pass.
Seventh: Canada can produce abundance for all her people. There was no question about that.
Eighth: Inflation comes from having more money than goods and services. Not a word has been said about that. Yet if we wish to discuss inflation that is the point at which we must commence. This proposition is borne out by the best authorities now living.
Ninth: Canada now has vast amounts of goods no one can buy. She is equipped to produce immediately upon demand vast quantities more of many kinds. The distribution of money would immediately call forth more production. When the almost hysterical outbursts against inflation were in process, not a word was said about that-not a word. And yet that, sir, is the all-important point. If we spent $100,000,000, and by spending that money we immediately brought into existence $100,000,000 or more of goods, there would be no chance in the world of creating inflation- except a form of financial inflation, with which we can deal later on.
Tenth: Therefore, Canada can safely create, issue and use a great deal of money. There was not a word of discussion about that-with the exception of the outburst about inflation.

Use oj Canada's Financial Resources
I said a few moments ago that not one of my contentions was met or answered-not a single one. I ask the members of the government this question: Why in the world was the whole question sidestepped? That is a vital point. Yet we have news sent clear to Australia stating how the Minister of Finance showed that social credit would result in inflation, that it would be most disastrous, and all that sort of thing. The Minister of Finance did not prove that at all, and he cannot prove it.
This debate has proved that $80 can be created in Canada for $1 of gold. It has proved that it can be created out of nothing but paper and pen and ink. That has been proved abundantly on the floor of this house. That is a wonderful achievement. The banks create all the money and they can beat the printing presses any day. We raise our hands in holy horror at the thought of printing presses, but we let the banks go ahead creating money far faster than the printing presses ever could. The banking system of Canada is the power plant that has been erected to serve the country. If we know how to use it we can change our streams of goods and services that are pouring through this country into money that can be used for the betterment of the country. But we must prove that we can do this.
A few moments ago I referred to turning water power into electricity. The first important point is to learn that water power can be turned into electricity. That was the question with which we were occupying ourselves and it had nothing to do with any of the other matters. Can we have money? 

that is the question. I understand that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) rose in his place and said that it was impossible for us to get money in any other way except by borrowing or by taxation. That is the stand normally taken in Canada to-day, but it is a stand which is utterly not in accordance with the facts. As long as we continue to take that stand, we will continue to be bound and the problems of this country cannot be solved.
The next question with respect to the power plant is that the amount of electricity developed depends on the volume and speed of the water. The amount of money that we can create depends upon the. volume and speed of our production and upon nothing else. Later on we shall deal with other matters. However, the Minister of Finance attacked it in this way. He did not stop to ask whether or not goods and services could be changed into money; he wanted to know immediately how to do it. If you came into the house
ready to discuss the question whether or not water power could be turned into electricity, and you were asked about the details of constructing a power plant, would you consider that to be a fair question? I do not wish to be unfair, but I speak as I see it. This is the next question: He said we do not need electricity; in other words, we have enough coal oil and we do not need any electricity.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I never said any such thing.
I shall make it abundantly clear to my hon. friend in just a minute. I am simply using an illustration.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend has no right-
Let me make my point first.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend says that the Minister of Finance said that we do not need electricity. The Minister of Finance never said any such thing and my hon. friend cannot put words into my mouth.
I am simply giving an illustration. If the Minister of Finance cannot follow figurative language, it is too bad.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend can use all the illustrations he likes, but he cannot put words into the mouth of an hon. member which that hon. member did not utter. I used the English language and nowhere did I use such words as those now attributed to me.

The point is this: The Minister of Finance argued that the A plus B theorem was faulty and there was no deficiency of purchasing power in the country as a result of industry. That is the same thing as saying that there was no need of electricity in the community. Why take all this trouble to create electricity? If that is not sufficient, I will take it all back. The trouble is the Minister of Finance did not allow me to finish what I was saying.
Speaking figuratively again, the next statement was that electricity will kill people, it will burn them-inflation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Who said that?

It was said that the new money would create inflation, that that would mean disaster and chaos. That is the same as saying that electricity would bum people and kill them.

Use of Canada's Financial Resources

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As long as it is clear that I did not say that, it is quite all right. My hon. friend is saying that, not I.

The next question
was that you cannot get a transformer, you cannot get a fuse plug to enable you to control the electric current after you create it. Therefore, do not create it. The objection there was to the just price.

Will my hon.
friend tell us now what he refused to tell us a few weeks ago? Who will be the transformers? Who will be the experts?

Would my hon. friend permit me to finish without interrupting? I do not remember the exact words of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Usley), but I got the impression that he was saying that the Minister of Finance had demolished completely our contention because he had brought in this A plus B theorem. The Minister of Finance demolished nothing by bringing that in. The hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) dealt unchallengeably with the A plus B theorem, as reported on pages 1304 to 1308 of Hansard. Any hon. member can turn up those pages and find what was said. If you turn to page 19 of the New and Old Economics you will find Major Douglas' reply to Professor Copland of Melbourne and Professor Robbins of London where the same argument is made.
Then about the banks in the west. The right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) made a remark which I think implied that we were endeavouring to discredit the banks. That is not the point at all. Our point in discussing the banks is to show that they create money, that they do not lend savings. The banks are teaching the people that they lend savings, and the fact is that they do not lend savings. As soon as the people realize that this is so they will begin to say, "Why should we owe and pay interest on this credit which they have created?" That is the first intelligent question about money that men will ask. In our discussion we have tried to show what money is, where it comes from, how it comes and what makes it. We used the banks as an illustration to make those points clear to our people.
I should like to turn again now to the amendment. No one can honestly contend under the circumstances that the government is using the monetary resources of the country as they could be used. The only means used by this government to put purchasing power into the hands of the people is through exports, as far as I can make out. We assume

that unless you practically throw great quantities of goods away in order to get rid of them, you cannot use any goods of that kind. Such an argument is a monstrosity. The only other means of providing purchasing power that we are using are relief, pensions, public works and rearmaments. I contend that we must use another .means to put purchasing power into the hands of the people.
In his speech the minister first of all proceeded to give us a fine outline of the banking system. I believe the people of Canada owe 'him thanks for doing that, because it is one of the finest things ever put before us by a public man in this dominion. I appreciated it tremendously. He then turned to a discussion of the proposals of the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker), just as though they had something to do with my motion. Why bring him in? I was not ready to meet what had to be said about him. As a matter of fact, the proposal made by the hon. member for Rosthern is not a social credit proposal. His proposal has merit, but it also has its difficulties, and it is not social credit. He proposed that an additional amount of Bank of Canada notes be created to carry on projects of various kinds. The Minister of Finance applied the principle of ten to one to show that we could reach such a tremendous amount of deposits in the banks as six billions of dollars, and he said that that would immediately cause inflation. I will grant that a great amount of money in a country might cause inflation, but in the United States they have over ten billion dollars of gold hidden in their vaults, and is that causing inflation? Of course not. Why? Because it is being handled right. You do not have to have inflation just because you have great quantities of money.
Under our present set-up, money cannot possibly get into circulation unless someone will come and borrow it. At the present time we are told the banks are full of money, and they cannot lend it to anybody, and they will not lend it. The result is that they are buying more government securities. Now will someone who thinks he knows tell us how, if you had six times as much money in the banks as we have now, you could get any more people to come and borrow it or get any of the banks to lend it? It has not been proved; maybe it can be proved, but certainly it was not proved. The question is, who would get the money? And again, where would they invest it?
Next there was an attack upon social credit. I am not going to deal with that at all at the present time because there are other

Use oj Canada's Financial Resources
matters which need attention. We did not bring social credit into the debate at all. We did not even mention the words social credit -not once.
Why not?

There is a scriptural quotation which could be used, but I shall not quote it now. We did not bring social credit into the debate at all because we had not reached the point where we were ready to consider the details of social credit. We were rather considering the question whether you could take the energy in our productive stream and convert it into money, because until you get that principle settled it is idle to take up other points of social credit.
Then the hon. member (Mr. Dunning) demanded concrete results. He said: These are only principles. But Mr. Speaker, before mankind could fly, you had to show men that it was reasonable to suppose they could fly, and we were simply discussing whether it was reasonable that Canada should be able to fly -that you could get electricity out of this great stream that is flowing by. That is what we were contending, and when that question is discussed openly, sincerely and frankly, hon. members will find that we shall be ready to take up other principles of social credit.
With respect to the speech of the Minister of Finance and the principles he enunciated, he said in the first place that money should be issued according to the needs of business. That is absolutely right, and I say that the real cause of the trouble in Canada to-day is that this government is not doing that very thing, and it cannot show that it is doing it. There is a great deal of agitation apparently for the purpose of making it appear that social credit principles are mysterious and difficult of understanding and all that sort of thing, that social credit would change everything, disrupt the whole of society. That is just pure nonsense. I am told that the Wright Brothers, in order to perfect the aeroplane, had to discover just one simple thing, and that was how to warp the tips of the aeroplane's wings. Everything else was there. And we contend, Mr. Speaker, that everything else that is necessary for social credit is here, that all that is required is just a slight change.
What is that?

There will be plenty
of time to develop that. What business needs above all else in this country to-day is that there shall be markets. If you could manage 51052-119
to give an adequate dividend to every man in this country, you would take care of markets inside of a month; and if you bring in the just price principle you would take care of the problem of a stable price to a tremendous degree. To bring about prosperity we must have an even price level. The best thinkers realize, and have done so for hundreds of years, that you can take care of the price level mainly by the amount of money in circulation.
Next, business wants lower taxes. If the government could manage somehow or other to create money to finance some of the things which are breaking the backs of the taxpayers to-day, it would remove a great deal of t's trouble with business; and it can be done.
The question of inflation was also raised. I maintain, sir, that there is no inflation in the .social credit contention. Major Douglas has stated time and again that he is entirely opposed to inflation. The only way in which you can possibly prevent inflation is by the introduction of social credit. I know there are many people who will say that that is not so; but that is so. And if I had more time I could read quotations from great authorities who cannot be questioned. I will refer to just one on this point of inflation. I quote from Paul Einzig, the great world economist, in his book World Finance Since 1914, published in 1935, where at page 17 he says:
The more advanced definitions (of inflation) duly allow for any change in the volume of real wealth. Thus if the volume of currency and credit increases, and the production of real wealth increases in the same proportion, then there is no reason why the expansion of currency and credit should produce an inflationary effect.
Is not that just as clear as it could be for him who runs to read?
Money properly distributed does cause more goods and services to come into being; where there are plenty of goods the money can be expanded, and it must be expanded. Otherwise, you have a fall in prices; you have deflation. That can be proved by reference to any number of authorities right down to the present moment. I have not time to refer to them all, but I am going to refer to Paul H. Douglas, professor of economics at Chicago, and his book, Controlling Depressions, written in 1935. I will give hon. members the page number, to save time-page 137. There he points out that when you increase the money in circulation you automatically increase goods and services, because there are vast quantities of unused resources, great numbers of men unemployed, great amounts of productive equipment being only partly used, and the minute you distribute money

is exhausted.
If I might have just a few minutes more, Mr. Speaker-
Go on.
I appreciate greatly the courtesy and consideration of the house, Mr. Speaker. There is a great deal to be said. I know the members want the facts, and I am glad to give them.
Time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think I was responsible for depriving the hon. member of five minutes of his time, but I do not think more than that.
By unanimous consent.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I had the impression that the house had given consent.
If hon. members will turn to G. D. H. Cole's Principles of Economic Planning, page 208, they will find the same principle set out there. The Minister of Finance assumed inflation. If you will go through his remarks with great care I believe you will find that every time he assumed inflation he at no time proved it. He told of the dangers that would come from inflation but he nowhere proved that inflation would come.
There is one other matter that I wish to deal with in the five minutes that have been granted to me; and if we are going to use the time let us use it without much disturbance.
A good deal was made of the question of the velocity- of circulation, and it was implied that social crediters are not aware of the principle of the velocity of circulation. That is entirely untrue. We have not discussed velocity of circulation simply because we have not got around to it. Let me read something that will interest the minister tremendously- a quotation from Professor Irving Fisher:
The latest and best studies on velocity show that in normal times it varies little; and even in booms and depressions its variations are much smaller than usually supposed, except for speculative transactions.
There are many people who imply that we quote out of context, and actually accuse us

of doing so, and for that reason I wrote to Professor Fisher, before quoting this passage, to ask him where it could be found. On March 19 of the present year he wrote me a letter in the course of which he said:
I do not now recall where the quotation from me on page 10 came from and I cannot now at this time make a search but it correctly states my views.
That is from Professor Irving Fisher of Yale, one of the world's great economists.
I have other material that bears upon the question, material of considerable force, but I have not the time to-day to discuss it. There is one question, however, to which I would refer here. Whenever the question of increasing money is brought up somebody rises and cries "Germany!" If hon. members will consult World Finance Since 1914 they will find at page 67 a complete statement explaining why Germany's issue of money failed. I contend that there is not one of those factors existing in Canada to-day-not one. Let hon. members read the book and form their own conclusion.
I greatly appreciate the extra time given me and the courtesy shown me. I submit that we were thoroughly justified in moving this motion of want of confidence in the government on the ground that, all things considered, the government has not adequately used the resources at its disposal to remove poverty from the midst of the Canadian people.

I refuse to be associated with any hon. member in this house in the view that banks, whether chartered or central, can in practice elevate one cash dollar to ten dollars in credit, or do this in any other way than theoretically under present practice. I intended to speak on this and cognate matters, but the unusual progress of the debate precludes the possibility of that. I shall, however, bring my statements before the house on another suitable occasion.

What is this about?

speakeroldname: Hon. T. A. CRERAR (Minister of Mines and Resources):
speechtext:
In 1927 a tripartite arrangement was entered into between the federal government, the government of New Brunswick and the government of the United Kingdom for the settlement of certain British settlers in New Brunswick. Under that agreement the. New Brunswick government supplied the land and the British government, as I recall, supplied the money for equipment. The part played by the federal government was relatively small; my recollection is that it was confined to a share of the interest losses that might arise in the first two years. That arrangement continued until 1935, when a new agreement was made between the federal government and the New Brunswick government under which the federal government in effect purchased the land from the New Brunswick government, covered by such settlers as were still on farms at that time. The understanding was that the New Brunswick government would be paid by the federal government as collections were received from these settlers. During the difficult period since then the payments have not come in from the settlers except in very small degree; consequently the liability is still outstanding to the government of New Brunswick so far as the federal government is concerned.

There is this further aspect of the matter, that we are paying five per cent interest on our obligation to the government of New Brunswick, and it has been considered advisable that it be closed out as at March 31, which is to-day. This vote is necessary for that purpose. I might add that originally there were 359 settlers, of whom 240 are or were recently still on these farms in New Brunswick. Of the amount of $572,975.01 the sum of $521,000 was really principal as at the time in 1935 when the new agreement was made. The balance represents accrued interest from that time to the present.
The amount was in fact borrowed, was it not, by New Brunswick in the first instance on their credit; then they bought the farms and sold them to the settlers?
I cannot say whether the amount was borrowed.-from the federal government?
No, borrowed from the public.
That is correct. At any rate New Brunswick found the money in 1927 to carry out its part of the bargain, either by taxation or by borrowing.
I was wondering whether we should take any steps to see that the money we thus pay goes to liquidate the outstanding obligations, because the money was borrowed for that particular purpose.

Just offhand I think that
might be inadvisable. New Brunswick might charge us with an undue interference in their affairs.

I was just wondering
whether there was anything in the nature of a trust as far as they were concerned with respect to that money.

No, I understand not;
but after all the responsiblity is with the province of New Brunswick to look after its own financial obligations.

that information. I did not come prepared to answer a question of that type, or a question such as that asked by the hon. member for Weyburn. I had intended raising a question under this item on a subsequent occasion, but I think it is well to take advantage of the first opportunity that presents itself to deal with one aspect of conciliation which I think is of considerable interest. I am sorry I could not give the minister advance notice of my intention to raise this question as in that event he probably would have had full information before him. My question concerns a dispute between the employees and the management of the Canadian Press which has been pending for some time. It seems
that they are farther away from settlement at the present time than they were when the dispute first started several months ago. From information I have received it appears that the management has taken rather a highhanded attitude toward the employees and has refused consistently to recognize their organization. I have seen their representatives who have been in touch with the Department of Labour; but it seems that there are certain formalities to contend with, which, instead of having the effect of bringing the parties to a closer agreement have had the tendency of creating difficulties in the attainment of that particular objective.
The Canadian Press is a semi-public organization, and we would have thought that its management would have set a better example to the rest of the country than it has. Difficulties have been placed in the way of the employees organizing, and the employers will not recognize the organization or union which has been formed. In December of last year the employees sent a memorandum to the employers, and in view of the fact 'hat there is before parliament a bill introduced by the leader of our group, having a direct bearing on this question, perhaps it would not be out of place if I read a few extracts from the memorandum. This is a memorandum prepared by the employees and submitted to Mr. Livesay of the Canadian Press:
This committee, representing your telegraph employees, requested this conference for the purpose of formally seeking acknowledgment and recognition of our right to organize and to bargain collectively with the Canadian Press through representatives of our own choosing.
And further:
_ To reach this common ground we believe it is essential the employees be organized, as the Canadian Press is organized, to permit representatives from both sides to meet as occasion warrants to discuss and agree upon terms of employment.
To reach this common ground we believe it is essential the employees be organized, as the Canadian Press is organized, to permit representatives from both sides to meet as occasion warrants to discuss and agree upon terms of employment.
However, we believe you will agree with us when -we say that the Canadian Press has been organized and developed primarily in the interests of its members who make up the Canadian Press. In other words, for the benefit of the employer.
We believe our desires in these respects can only be properly approached and considered if we are organized and are granted the right to bargain collectively through our chosen representatives.
That is why we respectfully request the Canadian Press to approve our right to organize and to extend us the right to bargain collectively.

Further on in the same submission they state:
We believe a union agreement between the Canadian Press and the employees will prove mutually beneficial.
Such an agreement, when negotiated, would represent the best possible conditions and terms of employment that can be established.
I could go on and give quite a number of similar quotations from the submission of the employees asking their employers to recognize the fundamental right of the employees to organize into a union of their own choice. This submission, which was made to the employers on December 7 last, was refused by the company, and now, as a result of the terms of the conciliation act as it stands at present, the employees are compelled to take a strike vote before the Canadian Press need agree to a board of conciliation being appointed.
I should like to state the case of the employees in a little more detail to show what a strong case they have for organization. In Canada, employees in certain categories who are known as junior punchers receive an average wage of approximately S22.50 a week, and senior punchers receive approximately $30 a week. In this country their hours of labour are forty-eight hours' a week. I want to compare these wages with those paid in the United States, and give the hours of work there. Wages for junior punchers in the United States are $45 a week, as against $22.50 a week in Canada, and senior punchers in the United States receive $52.50 a week as against $30 a week in Canada. In the United States they work from 36J to 41 hours a week, as against 48 hours a week in Canada.
The men who are asking for recognition of the right of the employees to bargain collectively are members of' the same international trade union as those who receive these tremendously higher rates of wages in the United States. But when the employees in this country attempt to band themselves together for the purpose of submitting their claims collectively to the Canadian Press, they are met with all kinds of obstacles, technicalities and difficulties when they request that a board of conciliation be appointed. I understand from the information which I have received, and which I think is reliable, that the Canadian Press has refused to accept a board of conciliation until such time as the employees have taken a strike vote on whether they will go out on strike to enforce improved conditions of employment.
One point I am trying to make is that I do not think it should be necessary for the employees in their organization to be com-

pelled to go to the length of taking a strike vote before the Department of Labour will grant a board of conciliation. If a strike vote is forced on the employees, it only tends, I think, to create greater difficulties subsequently than would be the case if the board of conciliation were appointed without this necessary formality of a strike vote. I know the viewpoint of the department, and I am quite sure that had they been in a position to grant the employees a board of conciliation without a strike vote being taken, this would have been done. But in view of the circumstance that the department is not in a position to grant a board of conciliation in this case without the formality of a strike vote having first been taken, I would ask the minister if some ways and means could not be found of amending the existing act or regulations to give the department power to grant a board of conciliation without this formality of the employees having first to take a strike vote.

As my hon. friend has just stated, he advised me only a moment ago of his intention to bring up this question at this time. It is quite true that there has been a dispute between the Canadian Press and some of its employees.
What class of employees?

The teletype operator. It was the hope of the department that it would be found possible to settle this dispute by direct negotiation. As a matter of fact, it is my own view that whenever these disputes can be settled by direct negotiation and collective bargaining, it is desirable that they should be so settled. But as my hon. friend has stated, apparently there has arisen a difficulty which is not capable of settlement by direct negotiation, and application has been made for a board of conciliation under the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act. That application is now pending, and I am sure it will not be expected that I should make any statement at this time with respect to the merits of the controversy. That would be wholly improper, but I can assure my hon. friend that the application will be dealt with on its merits. Certainly there has been no intention on the part of officials of the Department of Labour to place obstacles in the way of having this application granted.
As perhaps members are aware, it is necessary, in order to avoid the setting up of boards sometimes for frivolous purposes, to require that certain declarations shall be made in connection with the application, and one of those declarations is to the effect that

Supply-Labour
unless the dispute is adjusted or a board is set up there is a reasonable and probable belief that a strike will ensue. That, after all, is the reason why the Department of Labour sets up a board in such cases, to prevent a strike in industry.
Is that equivalent to what is known as a strike vote?

A strike vote is commonly taken. I can assure my hon. friend of that, although I have not the statute before me. As perhaps will be recalled, a strike vote was taken at a later stage in connection with the dispute last year between the railway companies and their employees. I should like to say, however, that under the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act a board can be set up without the consent of both parties. As a matter of fact, that has been done within recent months in a dispute which arose in the Minto coal fields. At the same time it is always desirable that both parties to a dispute should cooperate in selecting the personnel of the board. I am sure my hon. friend will appreciate the importance of that, and therefore the department believes that if and when this board is established, it will have the full cooperation of the management of the Canadian Press with respect to the nomination of a representative of the employers concerned.
I would emphasize that I have no complaint at all in this particular case against the Department of Labour.
I am just making the point that the application is pending and will be dealt with on its merits.
Has the department, in the minister's opinion, the legal right to establish a board against the consent of one of the parties to the dispute?

What can be done under one section of the act is to set up a board on the initiative of the minister. When that is done, we still ask both parties to the dispute to make their nominations to the board; but if one of the parties should refuse, that nomination can be made at the instance of the Minister of Labour. I mention that because that situation arose in recent months in connection with the dispute at Minto. The board was set up by the minister. The employers concerned declined to make a nomination, and the nomination was made by the minister in order to complete the personnel of the board.
Have any objections been raised?
In the Minto case objections were raised, but they were not pressed. The board was set up and has functioned.
The Snider case made it clear that jurisdiction with respect to some phases rests entirely with the provincial authority.
Yes.

It would be competent for the province to set up a board under the decision in the Snider case. We are operating under a sort of modus vivendi so far as the general application of the act is concerned.
After the decision in the Snider case was rendered, the provinces passed enabling legislation.
Not all of them.

Not all of them, but the majority did; and it is under that enabling legislation that the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act has functioned with respect to provincial undertakings or public utilities operating wholly within the boundaries of one province.

This act is not as useful as it used to be in industrial cities. For example, three people came to me with regard to applications. There is concurrent jurisdiction, the Ontario government having a department that does almost similar work. That department uses the conciliation and labour office for the same purpose. Has there been any overlapping since last year or the year before? I thought there would be a good deal less work. I had some correspondence with the labour department, and they referred me to the labour and conciliation department of the province. I wonder if there has been any falling off in applications from, 'say Toronto.

I have not that information before me at the moment; but I would say that as a result of the setting up of conciliation services in the larger provinces, particularly in Ontario and Quebec, there has been a moderate reduction in the work done by the conciliation officers of the federal Department of Labour. There are quite obvious reasons for that change. In both Ontario and Quebec, within recent years boards have been set up to deal with the regulation of wages. That has established a much closer contact between provincial authorities and labour and industry in general. Not only that, but some of the disputes that occur are referable in part to decisions which have been given by fair wage boards in the provinces. In this connection I might refer to the fact
Supply-Labour

that disputes have recently occurred in Cornwall in the plant of Canadian Cottons, due in some part to a misunderstanding with respect to wage regulations which were put into effect by the wage and labour board of Ontario. The dominion Department of Labour enters a dispute at the invitation of the parties concerned. It is always ready to send a conciliator to deal with a dispute under those conditions; but where a dispute occurs in a province that has its own conciliation service, we do not as a rule intervene when the conciliator of the provincial department is dealing with the situation. I think the reasons are clear why it is not desirable that there should be intervention under such circumstances. We try to avoid duplication and conflict as between the services of the two departments. The chief interest of both departments is, of course, to settle disputes; the desideratum is cooperation between the departments involved.
One is a compellable jurisdiction and the other is not.
Yes.

Under the act the dominion government, through the head office, supplies forms to all employment offices, and during the past year there has been an unusually heavy demand. There is not a dominion employment service distinct from the employment service that operates in the various provinces. The employment service of Canada is provided for under the Employment Offices Coordination Act, which provides for an annual grant of $150,000. This amount is paid to the various provinces to assist them in establishing or maintaining a coordinated system of employment offices across the dominion.
Following the judgment of the supreme court, they were provincial and we undertook to assist them.

The function has always been recognized as a provincial one; but after a number of employment offices were established in several provinces, it was decided that it would be of advantage to have the

various services coordinated, and in 1918 this was brought about under the Employment Offices Coordination Act. From that time forward the dominion government has paid a grant in aid of $150,000, divided among the several provinces to assist them in maintaining employment offices. The dominion branch is a clearing house for information and assists in the transfer from one province to another of those seeking employment. It provides forms to all employment offices, so that one might say that the service is cooperative in character.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS

speechtext:
Hon. NORMAN McL. ROGERS (Minister of Labour) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to provide assistance towards the alleviation of unemployment and agricultural distress, and for such payments out of moneys appropriated by parliament as may be necessary for all or any of the purposes of the proposed legislation.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Sanderson in the chair.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
This resolution precedes the introduction of an annual bill for the relief of unemployment and agricultural distress. The bill when introduced will be similar, in general terms, to the Unemployment and Agricultural Assistance Act, 1937, which expires at the close of this month.
Under the terms of the legislation, and subject to the appropriations made by parliament for the purpose, provision is made first for the initiation and execution of works and undertakings by the dominion government, in order to relieve unemployment and agricultural distress and, second, for financial assistance to the provinces, under appropriate agreements, in order to assist them in their efforts to deal with unemployment needs and also the serious conditions which have arisen in certain sections of the prairie provinces because of prolonged drought.
I realize fully that it will be the desire of members of the house to discuss the unemployment question at some length before the Easter recess, and with this in mind, on second reading of the bill which will be introduced following the approval of the resolution, I intend to make a full statement on behalf of the government. We propose to move second reading of the bill on Monday. Meantime, it is intended to-morrow to table and distribute the final report of the national employment commission. That, again, seemed

Belief and Agricultural Distress
to be a good reason why it was best that my statement should be deferred until hon. members had enjoyed full opportunity to read the report of the commission.
In these circumstances I feel I may fairly ask for the cooperation of the committee in expediting passage of this resolution in order that we may proceed on Monday with the second reading of the bill.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
This seems to be a strange procedure. I have no desire to delay the regular business of the house; but it seems to me that the report of the national employment commission should be in our hands before the resolution is placed before the committee and, further than that, that the time to make the full statement the minister promises is during the discussion of the resolution, and not afterwards. Members of the committee are at this time in a position intelligently to discuss the resolution.
This resolution and the bill which will be founded upon it deal with the most important matter which has come before the house this year. It would seem to me highly desirable that we take no step whatever until the fullest information is before the committee, and therefore I take this opportunity to protest against this procedure. I am afraid that members in this little corner will have to ask the minister to make his statement before he may expect us to pass the resolution.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
I suggest to the minister that on the introduction of the resolution it would be appropriate to make a comprehensive and complete statement of policy, and a review of conditions in connection with unemployment. To many hon. members the legislation coming down will be the most important of the session. Unemployment has been with us for at least seven years, and I believe that, as on second reading of a bill we are limited to a discussion of the principle involved, there should be a more complete and comprehensive statement than the minister has outlined, or has intimated he intends to make to-night.
The principle of the bill will be a provision for the relief of unemployment. I am sure no hon. member would disagree with such a principle. Therefore, perhaps our discussion on that occasion would be to some extent limited. I am sure the minister is in a position to-night to review the legislation adopted by parliament during the seven years to which I have referred, and no doubt he is in a position to outline in more or less detail what is proposed, and also to give us a fairly comprehensive statement of the work of the

employment commission. That commission has been working for a year. Does it suggest anything new? Is there any radical departure from the principles and methods adopted in the past five years in dealing with this question? What objectives has the government in mind? Particularly, how do those objectives differ in principle, if they do differ, from those which have been adopted in years gone by? Are we to have a supplementary estimate covering unemployment relief, and all that sort of thing?
I believe that in justice to the committee the minister ought at this time to make a fairly comprehensive statement along the lines I have indicated. I do not think anything else will satisfy the committee, and I believe the passage and understanding of the bill would be promoted by the timely and complete statement which the minister, with his accurate knowledge of conditions, could make.

I am entirely in the hands of the committee. So far as the question of procedure is concerned, may I say to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that in submitting the resolution in this manner I am following the practice established in two previous years. I am quite sure I am correct when I state that in each of those years the committee accepted the resolutions after brief discussion, and our debates on unemployment took place on second readings, and during the committee stages of the bills. I say that only to assure the hon. member that there is no desire on my part to deviate from well established practice in this regard.
On the other hand I fully realize-and it has again been brought to my attention by those who have just spoken-that it is most desirable that there should be at this time a full and comprehensive statement on unemployment conditions. It was and still is my intention to make such a statement. On the other hand, I did feel, and still feel, that if that discussion is to be profitable, it is desirable that it take place after, and not before the report of the national employment commission has been tabled and distributed. Under these conditions and with the desire to meet the wishes of the committee as fully as possible, I would suggest that the resolution remain in committee. I shall make my statement after the report of the national employment commission has been tabled to-morrow; that is, in accordance with my original arrangement, I shall make it on Monday of next week. If this meets with the approval of those who have just spoken, I shall move
