Item agreed to.
Governor General's Warrants, 1937-38-
To provide for the purchase and distribution of feed and fodder for live stock in the drought areas, and in rural municipalities and local improvement districts not included in the drought areas, of Saskatchewan and Alberta; for freight charges and for the cost of moving equipment used in providing feed requirements; also expenses of marketing cattle in the drought areas (Governor General's warrants of August 6, and October 29, 1937, and January 19, 1938). $13,750,000.

What supervision is given by the federal Department of Agriculture? I have had some complaints as to the quality of feed grain which has been distributed in some parts of Saskatchewan. I wrote to the minister this morning giving the details of one of these complaints, but of course he will not yet have received my communication. My information is that some of the grain shipped in was in such condition that the farmers hesitated to feed it to their hogs. I was wondering if the federal department is giving any supervision to the purchase and distribution of this grain or whether this work is being left to the local authorities. I should like to know whether complaints of
this nature should come to the minister here or be sent to the Saskatchewan Department of Agriculture.

In connection with feed and fodder, the federal government provides the funds to pay the accounts, while the provincial government makes the purchases. The federal government has a staff of approximately thirty to forty which checks the grain and fodder for the purposes of grading. Most of the fodder is graded where it is purchased, some of it being graded on the farm where it is located. The grain is graded at certain points through which the cars pass when it is not possible to grade it where it is purchased. This grading occurs at points like Moose Jaw and Calgary. It may happen that the grain was threshed under conditions which were not too good. There was considerable rain in Alberta during the threshing season, and also in Manitoba during the latter part of the season. Of course, grain that was loaded into cars in a damp condition might arrive at destination not in too good shape. If we consider the quantity that has been handled, there has been very little reported to us as having been in poor condition.
Two or three weeks ago I received from southern Alberta a sample which I would have condemned. I did not know all the circumstances, so I sent it back to have them checked up. I do not think any inspector should have passed this grain. Occasionally cars or parts of cars get by the inspection, but one must understand that the ordinary channels of trade for grain in western Canada are east and west. Grain moves to Winnipeg or Vancouver. When you start moving grain across the regular channels of trade, that is from the north of the province to the south, you must set up an organization for checking and grading purposes. All grading organizations are now located at Winnipeg or at the other end, and it has been found necessary to set up more or less temporary organizations. It is extremely difficult to make a proper check as would be the case if the grain moved in the regular channels.
I notice that this item refers to relief outside the drought area, and I should like to have a break-down of the figure. How much money was spent in Saskatchewan and in Alberta?

It would be difficult to give the exact amounts spent to date. The nearest I can get to that is to give the amounts which were provided. We entered into agreements with Alberta and Saskatchewan providing for maximum sums of money

Supply-Agriculture-Feed

that the federal government would supply for feed and fodder for relief purposes in certain areas. In the case of Saskatchewan, up to August 6, there had been provided $200,000 in one amount and $2,700,000 in another. Those are the amounts covered by the agreement, not what was spent to that date. Then in October, for feed and fodder in the federal area in Saskatchewan, there was provided $5,000,000, and $1,000,000 for the area outside what has been termed the federal area.
I Should like to know the amount of money spent outside the drought area.

I shall give all the figures and perhaps the hon. member can separate them. This may save repeating them later on: For feed and fodder in the federal area, $5,000,000; for feed and fodder outside the federal area, $1,000,000. For feed and fodder in the federal area in Alberta, up to the same date, the amount was $750,000. For feed and fodder, on the same date, outside the federal area, the amount was $100,000. On January 19, 1938, inside the federal area in Saskatchewan, the amount was $1,000,000. Those are the total amounts up to the vote of $1,000,000, under item 462, for feed and fodder, which we put through a few moments ago, and which has to be added. The other vote that we put through was for direct relief, which may be spent partly in Alberta and partly in Saskatchewan.

From the minister's figures it would appear that outside the drought area in Saskatchewan not much more than $5,000,000 has been spent, and yet there is a vote of $13,750,000. There seems to be a discrepancy somewhere, or the total amount has not been expended.
There is still $3,000,000 lot accounted for by feed and fodder. That s in the cattle vote. I understood the request was for the feed and fodder figures.
Certain farmers who did not cut down their stock were not eligible for the grant, I understand, and loans were made this spring or during the winter. Would they be included in this estimate?
No; the loans are not included in this estimate. These are the warrants for the amounts that were advanced by this government.
What items do the loans come under?

The hon. member has mentioned an amount of

$13,750,000 for local improvements not included in the drought area. What do the expenditures outside the drought area consist of?

The term "in and outside the drought area " is really a misnomer, as I was going to explain. One year ago in handling this matter, the plan followed was to some extent different from that followed this year. A year ago we took, on the first of September, a certain number of municipalities and accepted responsibility for them right through to March 31. We found by experience a year ago that it was extremely difficult to get decisions in the middle of the season. The provincial government would get an application from a municipality to be admitted to the area, and the province in turn would make application to us, and by the time the matter had been considered by three different authorities perhaps a month had gone by, while in the meantime people were having great difficulty. So this year we adopted a different system. We accepted at the first of September responsibility for all the municipalities that were admitted to the federal area. The federal government agreed with the provincial governments to take responsibility for 170 in Saskatchewan and fifty-three in Alberta from September 1 to March 31. We have accustomed ourselves during the winter to call that area the drought area. But outside and around the fringe of that area there are in Saskatchewan at least ninety municipalities, and in Alberta at least ten municipalities, which are in almost as bad conditions as the others. They are really drought area too; but probably it would not have been necessary to bring them in, if we had been dealing with the matter here, until the first of October in some instances, and the first of November, or the first of December, in others. They could have taken care of themselves to that time. So we said to the provincial governments that we would advance a certain cash amount to be used in those areas. In Saskatchewan the amount was $1,000,000, and in Alberta, $100,000.
The amount of $100,000 for Alberta was not our suggestion. We proposed $200,000 for Alberta, but the provincial government proposed an adjustment in the number of municipalities to be taken in and agreed to take half the amount of money for the outside area provided we made an adjustment. So we took in eleven municipalities that we would have preferred to leave outside the area for which we assumed full responsibility.
These amounts were set aside to assist in taking care of these people outside the area for which we took 100 per cent responsibility.

Supply-Agriculture-Feed
The provinces were administering the distribution of feed and fodder for the whole area, both the area for which we paid the entire cost and the area in which we gave assistance. So the set-up inside and outside is much the same, and the methods of administration the same; also any regulations governing persons who were obtaining assistance in the form of either direct relief or feed and fodder were intended to be the same. We made inspections to satisfy ourselves that the administration was the same inside and outside the area, once a community had been admitted in under relief.

I understand from the minister's explanation that owing to the type of supervision exercised, it is impossible to determine what amount has been spent in Saskatchewan and what in Alberta; that it is impossible to segregate the expenditures.

It is not impossible at all. As a matter of fact, when the accounts are completed there will be an exact division as between the two. There is no connection at all between the moneys spent in the two provinces. The Alberta government spent all the money provided for that province, and the Saskatchewan government spent all the money provided for that province. We are not spending that money; it is the provincial governments who are spending it through their own organizations. All we are doing is to make a certain check to see that the money is expended in what we think is the proper way and in accordance with the proper regulations.
The minister said that certain adjustments were made when Alberta agreed to ask for $100,000 instead of $200,000. What were those adjustments?

The adjustment was
this:	There were a number of municipalities north and west of Hanna, in the area between Hanna and Edmonton, in the vicinity of Coronation, which the provincial government desired to have admitted to the area. We had selected forty-two other municipalities that we thought, according to our investigation, should come in; but the province asked to have about twenty others around the fringe of the area taken in, and we increased the number from forty-two to fifty-three; that is, we took in eleven more. These municipalities were mostly in the vicinity of Coronation and down towards Drumheller.
So it was because some additional municipalities were included in the drought area that it was not necessary for Alberta to ask for an increased giant?

It was not a matter
of an increased grant. The amount we originally suggested which they should have for the outside area was $200,000. They said they would prefer $100,000 for the outside area and for us to .take in eleven additional municipalities for which the federal government would assume entire responsibility.
Does any part of these moneys consist of loans to the provinces to be repaid to the federal government?
No; they are grants to the provinces and are not repayable.

I regret that we have not had an opportunity earlier in the session of discussing this question of relief in Saskatchewan, particularly the distribution of feed and fodder. The minister will remember that in the debate on the address I brought to the attention of the government the critical situation in that province with respect to feed and fodder, and at that time I also drew his attention to the fact that early last fall I had taken this matter up with both the provincial Department of Agriculture and the federal Department of Agriculture here in Ottawa.
The minister will remember that, speaking on the address himself, he stated that he was more concerned about taking care of the situation in March than he was in having feed there in the fall months. In the last three weeks I have been receiving protests and certain information from Saskatchewan indicating quite a critical situation with regard to feed and fodder and grain to take care of the spring work. To-day I received a letter from a farmer in the Indian Head district suggesting that it is almost imperative for the government to see to it that the farmers are provided with tractors and tiller combines to get the crop in, because the horse power is very low. The horses returning from the feeding pastures in Manitoba are in no condition to tackle the spring work. I suggest that the minister give us a detailed statement regarding the quantity of feed and fodder supplied each month, starting with September, to the drought area and semi-drought area in Saskatchewan. We should also have a statement regarding the quantities obtained in Manitoba, Alberta, and the states of Minnesota and North Dakota.
The minister referred to-night to the inspection that has been made of the feed and fodder shipped in. As he said, some of it was not in very good condition. Of course, in Manitoba particularly, from which a good deal of it came, the season was such as to
Supply-Agriculture-F eed

make it difficult to turn it out in proper condition. If we consider the time it was cut and the delay in baling, the weather was such that some of it was damp. I saw some carloads that were shipped in before I left home and they were in poor condition. As the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar has said, the fodder was not fit to feed to animals that were expected to show any improvement. It was not fit for dairy cattle or for work horses. The minister has referred to the men inspecting the feed and fodder, for a list of whom I asked some time ago. I am referring to the inspectors whom he mentioned in his speech on the address-some forty-five of them. A return was brought down last week giving the names of some twenty, and I think he should give us the information with regard to the others. These are the men who are doing inspection work in connection with the distribution of relief.

I might deal with that point now. In my speech on the address I said that at the peak we would not have more than forty-five, and I found in answering the question that, as a matter of fact, we have never had more than thirty-five. At the time the question was asked there were twenty-nine, as the return shows.
This return shows twenty-eight.
Yes, twenty-eight.
After receiving that return I asked a question with reference to one of these men in particular, the man at Broadview.
Agnew.

Yes. Let me read from the
return:
Was A. S. Agnew of Broadview, Saskatchewan, employed in the purchasing of feed and fodder in Manitoba or Minnesota for the province of Saskatchewan?
The answer was that he was employed as a feed grader and used in Minnesota and North Dakota.
Not in connection with purchase, but as a feed grader.

Yes. The return goes on.
Employed from October 19, 1937, to February 21 1938. $125 per month plus actual travelling expenses as follows: October, $137,59; November, $303.52; December, $278.68; January, $205.97; February incomplete.
That man in four months drew some SI,400 by way of salary and expenses.
He does not draw expenses.
His expenses were paid.
The government paid his expenses.

Yes, and that means that by way of salary and expenses he has cost the country SI,400 in four months. I call that an outrage. There are all sorts of good men available to do such work at a far smaller cost to the country. Would the minister give us the number of other inspectors engaged in similar work. I suggest that he take this list and set out what each one of the inspectors has done, how many were employed in the purchase of feed and -fodder, and so on. I understood that there were one or two in Regina, but I do not see their names in the return. They had a commission, I understand, to go to Minnesota to secure feed and fodder, and I suggest that we should have a statement in that regard. Furthermore, the minister should give us a statement with regard to the number of cattle shipped out; the number shipped to different markets; the number shipped to the feeding ground; the number of horses shipped to the feeding ground and the number of those that have been returned. Were there any veterinarians employed in Manitoba to attend to the horses at the feeding grounds in Carberry? We should have all that information. The minister should tell us who these men are and give us their salaries.	_
I trust that the minister will not treat this request lightly.
He said the other evening that some of the matters I have mentioned were of no concern to this government; that they were of concern only to the Saskatchewan government. May I emphasize the gravity of the situation and the necessity for full information. It is regrettable that such information as we are asking for is forthcoming so late in the season. Early in February I asked for a return, which I suppose may be discussed under item 471, with respect to all commodities distributed in Saskatchewan for relief purposes, and only this evening has the minister been kind enough to hand me a volume containing the information. It covers from twelve to fifteen large pages, and no doubt we shall be asked to accept this document and pass upon it to-night. I must protest against this. The return was ordered on February 23 and I have just been handed it to-night. If the minister thinks we can go through this return hurriedly with regard to quantities of fish, beans and so on, the places of purchase and distribution; if he thinks it is fair to hand such information to us and ask us to consider it intelligently on the spur

Supply-Agriculture-Feed
of the moment, I do not think he will find anyone to agree with him. I suggest that at least the matter should stand until we have had an opportunity to study this return carefully and to ask for any necessary information in connection with it.
I should like to have a statement with regard to the amount of feed supplied each month from Manitoba and the United States, and the minister might tell us something about the pools' offer in connection with the distribution of it. A good deal of money could have been saved in that direction, and I think it important that we should have a statement. We shall ask for certain other information as we go along this evening.

As to the remarks concerning the return, I saw it for the first time after leaving the house this afternoon. It was placed on my desk to be brought down tomorrow, and I brought it with me to-night and gave it to the hon. member so that he would have it. In fact, he had it within a few minutes after I received it myself. So if there is any information with which he is not familiar, neither am I familiar with it.

Just there may I say that the order for this return was passed on February 23. It had stood for quite a while owing to the fact that the minister was out west, I am not saying on what business. One of the ministers asked that it stand until he returned; we allowed it to stand, and as soon as the minister got back it was passed. That was on February 23.

For much of this information we have to send to Regina. The inquiry had to do with work that was done partly in Regina; all the distribution was done there, and so the return could not be completed here.
In regard to the discussion generally, this is not the last opportunity that will be afforded this session of discussing all these matters. Before the session ends, we shall have to put through estimates having to do with supplies for similar activities, and full discussion can then be had of all these matters.
I can give the committee some of the information, although practically everything that has been asked for involves obtaining information from Regina or Edmonton; it is not information that we would have here in detail at any time unless we sent there for it. It has to do with administration of affairs by the provincial governments. We are concerned largely with two things: First, seeing that the accounts are properly audited, making sure that the money is spent for the purpose for which it was voted, and, second,
checking the activities to see that in the distribution of feed and fodder and direct relief proper service is being given to the area for which the money is being spent. Outside that we do not go fully into the detail. We receive from time to time returns showing what is being done; but to give the information in all the detail asked for by the hon. member would, I think, be impossible unless he is prepared to wait another two or three months while we get the information. I can, however, give in general terms the division, the amounts of money involved and the tons of fodder. The last summary I have is down to February 7.
On February 7 commitments in Saskatchewan were for 7,816,288 bushels of feed grain, of a value of $5,636,230.38. Amount under commitment at that time:	Requirements,
6,944.872 bushels; estimated for cash sale, 346,620 bushels; commitments, 7,816,288 bushels; leaving commitments in excess of requirements, 524,796 bushels. That is a complete statement for the federal area of the drought section of Saskatchewan as far as bushelage is concerned.
In the marginal area, that is the area which is outside what some people call the drought area but which is still in the drought area, the requirements are 2,403.462 bushels; estimated for cash sales-that is bushelage which is sold to people who pay for it-91,603 bushels; commitments, 2,206,738 bushels, leaving requirements in excess of commitments, 288,327 bushels of feed grain.
The commitments for fodder in the federal area to February 7 were 269,000 tons; requirements, 301,000 tons as estimated at that time, leaving 32,000 tons requirement over commitments. The commitments there mean the amounts for which municipalities have asked and which the government has agreed to supply.
In the marginal area commitments are 50,000 tons and requirements 58,000 tons, leaving 8,000 tons of requirements in excess of commitments to that time.
That is as near as I can get to the detail in regard to feed and fodder in Saskatchewan during that period.
So far as the two provinces are concerned, there is a difference in the amounts of money supplied, but there is also a difference in the number of people and the area involved. In Saskatchewan there are 438,000 people on direct relief. In Alberta there are 64,420 people on relief. In dealing with those figures, one must remember that there are many people who are getting feed and fodder for live stock who are not getting direct relief

Supply-Agriculture-Feed
To give them feed and fodder for their live stock is one of the means of keeping them off direct relief. So there will be an even wider difference in the figures for feed and fodder than in those for relief. A careful check of what is going on over the drought area indicates that there is somewhere between eight and ten times as much area, and between eight and ten times as many people involved in Saskatchewan as in Alberta. If hon. members follow these figures through carefully, they will see that there is just about the same proportion in the amount of money being expended in the respective areas in order to take care of people and live stock there.
In regard to such matters as shortage of power with which to put in the crop and other such complaints, I can only repeat what I said the other evening; it is strange that I should not be getting those complaints. The farmers' organization in Saskatchewan some months ago circularized all its locals, according to the letter they sent to me, asking them to make complaints if there was any cause of complaint, and not very long after that the bulk of the complaints ceased to come. I have not received any considerable number of complaints recently, and since in that area there are in the neighbourhood of 500,000 people involved, I consider it strange that there are not more complaints if there is so much dissatisfaction. But when complaints are received, I do this with them: I write back to the individual who makes the complaint and indicate that the administration is being carried on by the provincial government; that he will get quicker action on his complaint if he writes to Regina or Edmonton than he will by writing Ottawa; but that in the meantime I am sending his complaint on to the officials in Regina or Edmonton and asking them to deal with it as soon as possible. Possibly if hon. members would do the same, we would at least get the assistance to those requiring it at the earliest possible date, if they are not being properly treated now.

I hope the minister does not think I am trying to exaggerate when I say that we are getting plenty of complaints. I have under my hand at the moment fifty or sixty letters of complaint, and just to-day I received from the secretary of a municipality a letter in which he said they had been informed by the department at Regina that they would not get half of what was required in the way of feed for this spring. That is not one of the 100 per cent areas, of course, but I believe in many instances the situation is just as bad in the 100 per cent districts. So I am not exaggerating at all. If I wanted

to do so, I could produce at least fifty complaints of recent date.

Probably I could produce as many, more or less eulogizing this government and the provincial governments for the efficient way in which this work is being done; but I doubt very much if fifty letters from five hundred thousand people would prove anything one way or the other. An effort is being made by all the authorities, working cooperatively so far as possible, to have this particular job done. I can understand that members might at this time be receiving complaints from people who are a little anxious. The end of our financial year is March 31, and there has to be a cut-off somewhere in the payments that are being made by this government. Arrangements are being entered into as to those cut-off dates. That cut-off is the period between seeding activities and winter feed and fodder activities, and for that reason some people are wondering whether they are going to get sufficient feed and fodder to carry them through the seeding season.
The plans are that the feed and fodder in their possession now will be sufficient to carry them until about the middle of April, although the cut-off is at the end of March so far as the purchase and shipment of feed and fodder are concerned. An effort is being made to start the feed and fodder for seeding purposes moving immediately following April 1, in order to have it in the hands of the people by the time the other feed has been used up, and I think it will be found that there will be as little difficulty in connection with seeding operations as there has been in connection with winter operations. I do not want to leave the impression that everyone will be perfectly satisfied, but everything will be done to see that the work is carried on as efficiently as possible.

Is the required amount of
feed and fodder in sight? Is the government pretty well assured that it will be available?

I read the figures a few moments ago. I do not know how much they mean to the committee, but they mean a great deal to those who have been finding feed and fodder. According to these figures, between 350.000 and 360,000 tons of fodder have been obtained and shipped into that area from elsewhere. That is a great deal of fodder. We have never required in any previous year to ship more than 260,000 tons; I believe that was the greatest amount ever shipped into that area, and even in years when fodder was available right in the province, when practically all of it could have

Supply-Agriculture

Feed
been found within Saskatchewan for shipment to other parts of the province, it was very difficult to make arrangements to have that done in a way which would be satisfactory to everyone. This year scarcely any fodder was to be obtained anywhere in the province. It was necessary to go to Manitoba in the early part of the season in order to get fodder. Later on, it was necessary to go to Alberta, and I may say that in the early part of the season it was found very difficult to purchase fodder in Alberta because the authorities in that province wanted to make sure of their own supplies first. When eventually it was possible to purchase fodder in Alberta, and after everything possible had been done in those two provinces, they still were unable to get a sufficient supply. The next place they went was the state of Minnesota. Arrangements were made to get supplies, largely of hay, there. The only reason they went to Minnesota was because at that time the freight on hay from the province of Ontario to Regina was SIS a ton. Anyone knows that you cannot feed any animal a ton and a half to two tons of hay when the freight alone, apart altogether from the purchase price of the hay, is $18 a ton.
The first move made by the government of Saskatchewan was to go into the border states of the United States, where the freight rates would be low, buy hay and ship it into that area. But even after they had purchased all that they secured in those states at reasonable prices, they did not have sufficient. Then we brought further influence or pressure to bear on the railway companies in order to get the rates on feed from eastern Canada reduced. It was finally agreed to set a freight rate of $10 a ton on hay from anywhere west of Montreal to the drought area of Saskatchewan, and $10.50 from east of Montreal as far as Three Rivers. A similar arrangement was made in regard to British Columbia.
What was the rate from British Columbia?
It was $10.50 from east of Montreal and $10 from west of Montreal.
What was the special rate that was arranged from British Columbia?

There was a similar rate from British Columbia. So far as Saskatchewan was concerned the regulation was that they could not accept hay at a laid down cost in that province of more than $18 a ton, and under the special rate from British Columbia they were able to lay down hay for less than $18 a ton. They were also able to get hay
from the eastern part of Canada, under those special rates, for less than that laid down price.
I understood that the laid down price from British Columbia was $16 a ton; from Ontario, $17.50, and so on. Is that correct?

In that case I would say probably there was a difference of $1 or $1.50 in the freight rate from British Columbia as compared with the freight rate from eastern points. The only part we took in these negotiations was to assist the provincial government in getting special freight rates. They carried on all the other activities in connection with the matter. That was the case in regard to Saskatchewan. Alberta did not purchase outside the province.
What was the laid down price of hay and fodder coming in from the United States?

I could not give my hon. friend the exact figure; but it was considerably under that, probably in the neighbourhood of $15 a ton. It may have been as low as $14 from certain points in the United States, but I imagine the average would be somewhere around S15.
What was the average price paid in Manitoba?

The top prices that could be paid were set out in the agreement. The price for hay in Manitoba was $8.50 a ton; that was the top price which could be paid in western Canada for No. 1 hay, and then it was graded down to $6.50 a ton. The average price there would be somewhere between those two figures.
How much was purchased in the United States?

I have not the exact figures, but they would be somewhere between
75,000	and 100,000 tons.
What was the price paid for hay purchased in the United States ?

The price there was governed by exactly the same regulations that governed the price in Manitoba and Alberta. It could not be more than $8.50 per ton. It was under that price.
There is one further remark I should like to make. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle tonight made the statement he made previously in his speech on the address in reply, to the effect that some men had been paid commissions to buy hay in Minnesota. I believe at that time I told the house my information
Supply-Agriculture-Feed

was that no commissions were paid for purchasing hay in Minnesota; that the hay was bought in Minnesota at prices which were indicated in t'he agreements and sent up, and that no one in western Canada obtained a commission in connection with it. Some of it may have been purchased from agents in the state of Minnesota who had bought hay from farmers and who had it for sale, just as was done in Ontario and Quebec. The agents who had hay and straw sold that to the government of Saskatchewan. As to whether or not they made a commission, I do not know; I assume they made a profit. It is possible that men in Minnesota made a profit on hay purchased from farmers and resold to the government. But according to my information there was no commission agent acting for the government of Saskatchewan.
There was a great deal of hay purchased, though, was there not, from agents who had gone down to Minnesota from Saskatchewan, and who had accumulated quantities of hay there.

Not to my knowledge. There were men who went to Manitoba and Alberta, I assume-although personally I do not know of any who went there-and there probably were men who went to Minnesota and bought hay to ship to Saskatchewan. Some of that hay has been delivered to the municipalities, and the municipalities have sold it. As a matter of fact, I am buying hay this week, to put in my own crop, from a municipality which imported it from somewhere. I do not know from where it was imported. But I pay for the hay whatever it costs the municipality, plus freight and all other charges added. That has been done by municipal organizations throughout Saskatchewan, as a matter of convenience for the people in the municipalities.
There are no hay dealers in Saskatchewan, because we do not deal in hay. As a matter of fact, in the part of Saskatchewan from which I come we never feed hay. We have not done so in any year. But in a year like this, when we have to ship something in to feed our stock, it pays us better to ship in hay than to ship in straw or oat sheaves. There are no agents there to sell hay. There has to be an organization to do this, and the municipal organization is the one which is most convenient.
Someone may go to Minnesota or Manitoba, buy hay, and ship it in to the order of the municipality, and the municipality in turn may sell it.
-Mr. Gardider.]

How many checkers were employed in grading the hay? I assume there were checkers employed in checking provincial government accounts. How many checkers were there in Regina checking the accounts for the federal government?

The comptroller of the treasury has full control over the checking of accounts, and he has placed a few men at each capital. I have not the number in my mind at the moment, but I know it is a very small number, not more than half a dozen, and probably only three or four.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He puts men there as required.

Yes; he puts them there as required. At certain times there may be more than at others. So far as inspectors are concerned, may I say the hon. member has the list; at least he had it a few moments ago and was reading from it. It must be on his desk in front of him. I have not the list before me, but I do not think it would be of any use to read it. It means something to the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, and it means something to me, because we know some of the individuals.
That is fine, if the minister is willing to admit that the list I have is one of government inspectors.
That is what the list the hon. member has says.
And that they draw similar salaries. The information shows a salary of $125 a month, and expenses in some months running as high as $300.

I would say quite freely that the men on the list the hon. member has are all getting $125 a month, and they are all away from their homes. I think, if he will read the list, he will find they are nearly all farmers, and I think are all out of the drought area.
And all doing a good job.

Yes, all doing a good job. They all know hay when they see it; they all know grain when they see it, and they are grading fodder. So far as their expense accounts are concerned, this is made up of a charge of seven cents a mile and living expenses while driving around the country, locating farms where hay is available, and grading it. They must locate grain and grade it, so that when it leaves the point

Supply-Agriculture-Feed
from which it is to be shipped it may be known to be in proper shape. Then, we have other men at the other end who are checking to see that it arrives in proper shape.
Do they also locate where it is required?

No; the provincial
people locate the hay in the first instance. They locate it, and notify us that they have ordered a certain amount of it at a certain place, and we send a man there to grade and check it.
Is it the provincial government which receives the application for relief, in that regard?

The municipality receives the application for relief, and passes it on, through a committee of council, on which a representative of the province sits. Those applications are then submitted to the provincial governments. We never receive the individual applications here.

I appreciate the problem which must be involved in distributing upwards of $27,000,000 or $28,000,000 of relief, through governor general's warrants, as outlined in these various items. I believe that, despite our sympathies with the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta, all hon. members must agree that these are enormous amounts of money, and it seems peculiar that we should have items such as these, providing for " the purchase and distribution of feed and fodder for live stock in the drought areas, and in rural municipalities and local improvement districts not included in the drought areas, of Saskatchewan and Alberta; for freight charges and for the cost of moving equipment used in providing feed requirements; also expenses of marketing cattle in drought areas," and then, right below that, the item to provide for " direct relief expenditures," together with the items we have passed to provide for feed and fodder relief in the dried-out areas, and the further item to provide for direct relief in the dried-out areas.
That seems like a lot of items involving expenditures for the same purpose. What are the freight charges, and what is meant by " the cost of moving equipment used in providing feed requirements "? It seems to me that these items make it possible to provide relief or assistance in districts which are not in the drought area, and to provide money for the marketing of cattle and for the payment of freight-in fact for anything which may be wanted in that one province of Saskatchewan, whether or not the particular district is in the drought area. I do not
wish in any way to minimize the problem or the great crisis Saskatchewan has endured, but this seems to be an enormous amount of money. Very wide latitude is also given to the government to make expenditures in connection with those who are in drought areas, and others who are not.

I believe there is some confusion in the terms " in the drought area " and " out of the drought area." The meaning is exactly as I explained at the beginning of the discussion. What is known as the area " inside the drought area " is what came in after the first of September, and continued right through the year, and in connection with which the federal government pays the whole bill. But immediately outside that area there is another which is just as much in need of assistance as the area inside the line. We took 170 municipalities, and there are ninety municipalities immediately outside which are in almost as bad condition as the 170. Those are the meanings of " inside " and " outside."
There are similar areas in other parts of the dominion.

But not as compared with these. I do not think there are similar areas anywhere. I find from the information before me that in that area the bushelage is about two bushels to the acre, and a considerable part of the area of which I am speaking is immediately outside.
The other point had to do with moving the equipment necessary to provide the fodder requirements. Some of the municipalities maintained that they could send equipment to Manitoba, for instance, and put up this feed or fodder much cheaper than it could be bought anywhere else. This equipment would consist of balers and mowing equipment. We were asked to have the equipment sent down, and residents of the municipality were employed to go down with it to put up the fodder in the adjoining province or elsewhere within Saskatchewan. That fodder cost the government just the cost to the municipality of putting it up.
There are instances where this was the only way in which one could get fodder put up in a locality. During the harvest season all the farmers would be engaged in harvesting, and it was necessary to send men down from the locality where the hay was needed. It was also necessary to send down equipment as there would be localities where there was no equipment available. The province has a considerable number of balers. The idea was to ship down some of this government equipment along with the necessary
Supply-Agriculture-Feed

labour, put up the hay and ship it back to where it was needed to feed live stock during the winter. In these cases the government undertook to pay the freight on the balers and other equipment, and on the hay that was sent back.

What is
covered by expenses in marketing cattle? If the government pays relief to the farmer and provides feed and fodder for what cattle are left, what would be meant by expenses in marketing their cattle?

That is probably a long story, but that matter is covered by this item. There is 83,000,000 in this item that is not an expenditure; it is included in the first item of $13,750,000. In order to handle the cattle that were moved by the voluntary marketing set-up, it was necessary to have a revolving fund, which was provided by means of a warrant. Three million dollars of this money cover that fund. Probably I should give some information to the committee with regard to the plan followed.
How many were shipped in 1937?

I shall give that in a moment. In previous years we have had some difficulty in securing feed and fodder, but it was obvious to everyone at the beginning of the season this year that there was not sufficient feed and fodder in western Canada to feed the live stock that was there. I said during the debate on the address that we made arrangements for 70,000 farmers to keep about
280.000	head of cattle. A total of 280,000 head of cattle consuming a ton and a half per head means a considerable amount of fodder. This is covered by the figures I gave a few moments ago. We made provision also for the farmers in the same area to keep an average of nine horses each. Nine horses each for 70,000 farmers mean 630,000 horses. When you start to feed that many horses at the rate of a ton and a half to two tons of hay, you must have a considerable amount of fodder.
It will be realized that the amount of feed and fodder which we shipped in was not nearly enough to keep that live stock through the whole winter. Much of this fodder had to be got together by the farmers and a good deal was of a very poor quality. At the beginning of the season there were approximately 600,000 head of cattle in that area. We said that the farmers could not expect the government to take care of more than
280.000	head, and we hoped the people would get rid of the difference between that number and 600.000. Everyone realized that that was quite a task with the ordinary facilities

for marketing live stock, particularly when much of the live stock was not fitted for market. It was an impossibility to get rid of that much live stock without the farmers having to take a great loss while it was being done. So we decided to assist the farmers in the marketing of their surplus live stock.
Within a week of the time that we were convinced that fodder could not be obtained, we set up an organization. I am not going to maintain that no mistakes were made in setting up an organization to handle in the neighbourhood of 100,000 head of cattle. You cannot expect to set up an organization in a week's time to buy and sell that number of cattle without making any mistakes. There was recommended to us a Mr. O. Freer, living in the city of Winnipeg. At one time this gentleman had handled cattle for a cooperative organization and he was the secretary of an organization of stockmen. We asked him to take charge of the task of assembling and marketing these cattle and he agreed to do so. As I said a moment ago. he built up an organization within a week of the time when he was asked to do so.
Mr. Freer opened up an office in Carberry. He did this because, we were fencing something over 100,000 acres as a pasture at this point. We hoped to bring many of the feeder cattle to this point and he set up his office there. There was a Mr. Bailey who was acting as clerk, and a Miss Baker, as stenographer. He had a staff of graders and buyers as well, a list of whom I have before me. These men were paid S6 a day and expenses to go through the drought areas in Saskatchewan and Alberta to grade and purchase cattle. We asked the secretary treasurers of the municipalities to take charge of assembling the cattle. We agreed to pay the municipal organizations for the use of their secretary treasurers for the three jobs that we had to do during the two or three months of the season. One job was to assemble the cattle; another was to assist in distributing food that had been purchased in eastern Canada and British Columbia and shipped into the drought areas, and another was to assemble all information necessary for the distribution of feed and fodder within the municipality. The secretary treasurer was paid $125 a month for two or three months to do these particular jobs. He arranged to have the cattle assembled at two or three points in a municipality.
He advertised that we would pay the Winnipeg price, less freight, for all butcher cattle that were ready to go to the abattoir. We would pay the Winnipeg price at the initial point for all feeder cattle, and we

Supply-Agriculture-Feed
would pay 81.25 a hundred pounds for all canner cattle at the point at which they were assembled. With this information in their hands the individual farmers brought their cattle to the assembly points at which the grader and buyer graded them and bought them. The individual was paid cash on the spot just as though he had taken his cattle to the market. If the cattle were butcher cattle, they were taken to the abattoir in Edmonton, Winnipeg, Calgary, Moose Jaw or Regina. If they were canner cattle they were taken to various points and sold for what they would bring on the market at that time. The feeder cattle were sold on the stockyards to feeders from parts of the United States and other parts of western Canada or of eastern Canada, or were taken to the pasturage at Carberry and auctioned off to farmers who gathered there from eastern and western Canada. These farmers bought the cattle at auction and took them home, and if they shipped them to the east we paid half the freight on the cattle provided they kept them for three months before marketing them. We estimated at the beginning that we would require a considerable amount of money for this, but we found in the actual transaction that we did not require more than a fraction of the $3,000,000 included in the warrant provided in the supplementary estimates. The cattle were bought and sold. We bought 89.333 head of cattle.
They were shipped out of the district?

Yes; and the net purchase price of the cattle was 81,438,188.21; the net sales price was $1,250,102.07; so there was a loss taken of under 8200,000 on 89,333 head. In addition to that, there were freight charges which bring the total loss, in round figures, to 83.80 a head, or 8340,000.

That includes transportation
charges?

Transportation, administration costs and all netted a total loss to the government of 8340,000.
Mr.	ROWE	(Dufferin-Simcoe):	How
many of these cattle were shipped to the United States?

I have not the exact
figures, but it was a very small number. Most of these cattle went to the abattoirs in Winnipeg, Edmonton and Regina, and to eastern Canada.
Mr. ROWE	(Dufferin-Simcoe):	There
were a good many shipped to eastern Canada.

We estimated that
out of this group there would be 20,000 head shipped to eastern Canada as feeders, but many more were shipped that did not come into this group at all.
At present prices there will be another loss to absorb there.

Not on these cattle.
The feeder cattle were purchased at an average price of 817.31, so they will not take much of a loss on those.
It depends upon what the cattle were like.

They were good cattle
or they would not have been purchased as feeders. The poor cattle were all culled out, and the feeders were graded in carload lots at the pasturage. All the breeding cattle taken to pasturage were tested for T.B. and Bang's disease, and those who purchased them took them out of the area clear of disease. So I do not think anyone who took those cattle out at those prices is going to lose very much money.

As one fairly conversant
with the situation in western Canada, I want to take this opportunity of congratulating the Minister of Agriculture upon the really first-class job he did in handling the situation. His energy and sagacity in dealing with this great problem are, I think, highly creditable to any man in the Dominion of Canada. He mentioned Mr. Freer of Winnipeg, who had given him great assistance. I should like to take the opportunity of mentioning also Mr. Byers of Saskatchewan and Mr. Davies of Manitoba, two gentlemen who I believe, also gave great service. On a visit to Saskatchewan last year, I met buyers from the old province of Ontario. Cattle men can usually spot each other without wasting very much time-birds of a feather flock together, you know. In conversation with these men I found they all said that the system inaugurated by the minister was the cheapest and the best as far as they were concerned. They could go to Carberry and buy at auction, at their own appraisal, the cattle that suited them best, and they were thereby saved the expense of a trip through the country which might take a week to gather up a load of cattle. The only fly in the ointment, I think, is the fact that many of these cattle came to Ontario for feeding purposes. When they were purchased they were worth the money at that time, but owing to the slump in the market at the present time I think the farmers who are feeding these
Supply-Agriculture-Feed

cattle stand to lose some money or, at best, to break even. This is regrettable.
They will lose money.

They will lose, as the hon. member for Grey-Bruce suggests; on the other hand perhaps they made considerable money last year, and after all we make it one year and lose it the next. We have to take our chances as far as that is concerned. What I rose to say was that we appreciate the work which was done by the minister and his helpers in taking care of a grievous situation in western Canada.

I want to corroborate what
the hon. member for Portage la Prairie has said, but unfortunately I am afraid that the farmers of Ontario who bought these cattle are not going to make much money out of them. I understand that some of them are very much disappointed with the results, no matter what the trouble is due to. However, I did not rise to speak about cattle.
I want to ask the minister to give us some more information about the price paid for feed grain. He told us that 7,618,000 bushels of feed grain for Saskatchewan had cost $5,636,000. which is approximately seventy cents a bushel. I suppose a large proportion of this feed grain was either barley or oats, and if one looks at the market quotations which appear in the papers from time to time, and the price in Ontario, one will see that it is very much below seventy cents a bushel.

That amount included
the freight and shipping.

I suppose a large proportion
of this feed grain was purchased in Manitoba or Alberta, so the freight from these points would not be very great as compared with the freight from Fort William. I should like to know where this grain came from, where it was purchased and the price, and what difference in the price the freight made. Seventy cents a bushel seems a high price to pay with prices for oats and barley as they have been in the last six months.
That is feed wheat.
Yes, and in some cases it is fairly good.
It is a low quality wheat.

There was no feed wheat this year, but they estimate the cost per pound of wheat as against oats or barley or anything else, and ship in the feed that will give the best returns. There is a considerable amount of wheat and barley, some rye and more oats; but even oats at the present time in the district in which I farm will cost between sixty and seventy cents a bushel. We are not in the federal area. For oats that is the cheapest figure we can get by the time it is shipped in from Manitoba.
I have been buying oats shipped to my farm from western Canada at fifty cents.
I wish the hon. member could ship some of that back to Saskatchewan ; he must have had a preferential rate to get it down to that price.
That is the market quotation; I bought oats two weeks ago at fifty cents.

With reference to the remarks of the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe, I suggest that the hon. member for New Westminster could probably explain the question of freights much better than I can. If the hon. gentleman were living in the west, he would find that oats can be shipped from the centre of Saskatchewan probably to the middle of Ontario cheaper than it can be shipped from some places in Manitoba to some places in Saskatchewan. As a matter of fact, you can ship grain from Saskatchewan to China, according to what our friends on the coast say, just as cheaply as from Saskatchewan to Vancouver, if it is to be used in Vancouver.
That is right.

The same thing happens in connection with grain rates all over the west. If you start to ship grain across the routes that grain travels under the Crowsnest Pass rates, you will find that the freight rate is considerably higher when you ship a few hundred miles between points in western Canada than when you ship all the way to the port in the east. You cannot, therefore, gauge prices in Ontario on the basis of what we may have to pay for shipping grain north and south across areas in western Canada or for shipping from eastern Canada west into Saskatchewan.
With respect to the question of shipping cattle to the old country, earlier in the session some hon. member asked a question on the orders of the day with regard to this very matter, and I indicated then that we had three men in Montreal working on the question for about a week, two of them representing the Department of Agriculture and one the Department of Trade and Commerce. These men saw all the shippers and everyone who was interested in shipping cattle to the old country, and they brought back a report to us to the effect that the chief difficulty was the question of getting freight with which to fill the holds of the ships this year in order to make it possible to ship cattle on the deck at the rates at which cattle can be taken to the old country. The chief reason is that very little wheat is going from Canada to European countries this year; there was little wheat grown. Our recent reports indicate that that situation has been relieved greatly during the last few weeks.
The reports which I get from day to day are to the effect that even now it is questionable whether it pays better to ship cattle to the old country than to Chicago. At the time when we were first discussing the question the price was around five cents a pound. I do not know what prices are to-day, but within the last few days it was seven cents on the Toronto market. I venture to say that any of the cattle bought under the scheme we have been discussing to-night, which have been fed and can be sold at seven cents a pound, will make good money for the farmers who bought them. We had a man checking the stables of most of those who brought down cattle from the west under this scheme. There are approximately
20,000	head of these cattle that are being fed. We have also checked the stables of some of those who have cattle which they bought from men who went to the west and brought back considerable numbers hoping to make something out of them. Certain individuals brought as many as 14,000 head into certain areas of Ontario and resold them. Last fall they were sold at prices which looked reasonable, but I have no doubt that at the present price of cattle some of these men- perhaps most of them-will take a loss. That, however, has nothing to do with the cattle which came down under the scheme that I have been outlining. They were brought down from the west by people who did a good service to western Canada. They went and bought the cattle, brought them down and placed them on farms in eastern Canada. There are others who went west under the halffreight plan, bought cattle themselves throughout the area and brought them back, and they are feeding them. It is possible that some of them paid too much for the cattle and will consequently lose money.
We have been making every effort to get shipping space for cattle for the old country. At the moment there is available space for between 40,000 and 50,000 head. We could ship many more than that to the old country this year if it were possible to get space. The main difficulty is the fact that three years ago they wanted to ship 6,000; the year before last, 36,000; last year, 9,000, and this year they want to ship 60,000. Anyone who considers these figures will realize that it is impossible for shipping companies to prepare for a trade which varies to that extent.

The information which I received about three weeks ago was that space was available for about 40,000 head. The drovers tell me that they should have
Supply-Agriculture-Feed

space for about twice that number, and they say that bottoms are not available for shipping to the old country owing largely to the increase in the quota to the United States the year before, running to between 180,000 and 200,000 head.
We shipped about 300,000 all told.

Well, whatever the quantity was. They were diverted to the south. The story they tell me now is that the control of the space going to the old country is in the hands of three men, one in the old country, one in New York and one in Montreal. They are taking advantage of this situation to buy the cattle at the United States price, and bottoms not being available to ship them to the old country, the farmers have to take that price. The cattle stand them at the present time about five to five and a quarter cents a pound, some more than that, and they tell me they will lose not less than $10 an animal, which to Waterloo county will mean about $180,000. It is a serious situation. If that is right, and if this space has been taken up by three men and held in that way with the idea of beating down the price to the farmer, some action should be taken. I know the minister sympathizes with the situa- [DOT] tion, but cannot something be done to put a little pressure on to get these cattle across?

I have no brief for the three men who are shipping cattle and have the space; but as far as I have been able to find out, it is not a new thing, it has been the condition for many years. I think the hon. member for Kootenay East will agree with me that three men have controlled most of the space for a number of years. But they controlled it in the years when we were shipping 6,000 head and when we were shipping 60,000 head; they have had to take it both ways.
There is perhaps something more important to be done than merely getting control of the space that these men may have. Whoever had that space would have considerable difficulty in using it with satisfaction if we are to have such variation in the shipments of live stock to the old country. We may have to devise some plan to prevail upon our people to ship more regularly.
And ship fewer south.

It cannot be worked out in a moment. We have seen all the shipping companies that have space, gone fully into the matter with them, but have been unable 
to find any additional space in which cattle can be shipped to the old country at the present time to save anyone any money.

Not only is the situation serious this year; but if unfortunately the same conditions that we had last year should recur in western Canada, I think there will be a great deal of difficulty, after the recent experience, in having feeder cattle again brought to Ontario. I am sure the minister is doing the best he can; but I know a number of farmers in the county of Waterloo-and I am sure the Minister of Trade and Commerce will bear me out in this-who are going to lose a lot of money, and they will be reluctant to go into a similar deal again.

There is no doubt about the difficulty of handling the export of cattle to the British market. The minister is right in pointing out that the tendency which arises from time to time to abandon the British market in favour of the United States market when the latter market opens up is an old and serious difficulty affecting the continuity of supply to the British market. There is no doubt also that over a long period of years certain large exporters have substantially controlled the existing space on ships going to the old country. Of course they are in the business in a large way, and they give the shipping companies some assurance of continuity of freight. The difficulty comes about in this, that it costs a shipping company a substantial, sum to equip a ship to carry cattle, and when it is so equipped, that space is not suitable for general cargo returning to this country, so it is a handicap unless the supply of cattle moving to the old country is more or less regular. We found this condition back in, I think, 1931, and what was done at that time worked pretty satisfactorily and, I submit, might be again considered by the minister. The parliament of Canada voted a sum of money for equipping ships to handle cattle. If my memory is correct, this cost $14 a stall. Again speaking without the record, I believe a stall will accommodate three large animals or four small ones. The shipping companies were paid the cost of installation of these stalls, and we also took . pains to assure a certain number of cattle being shipped over a period of time, so that the shipping company was assured of a reasonable return for devoting that space to this class of business. In that way the records will show that we moved in certain years quite a substantial number of cattle.

You guaranteed them so many trips.

Supply-Agriculture-Feed

Yes. As a matter of fact the movement continued after that guarantee, and the movement of cattle was greatly facilitated. One unfortunate feature is that the small independent shipper, by the very nature of his operations, simply cannot guarantee continuity of supply. So the Department of Trade and Commerce joined with the Department of Agriculture in an effort to stabilize the supply by the smaller shippers, or made accommodation available to the smaller shippers so that supply could be guaranteed; and this greatly expedited the movement of cattle to the mother country.
In view of the circumstances mentioned to-night, it might be well to review the practice of those years and consider the advisability of again paying the cost of equipping ships for carrying cattle. The sum required was not large compared with the value of the service and the results achieved.
Back of it all lies this problem: The British market offers an excellent outlet for Canadian cattle, but we can hope to hold that market only if our cattle move forward with reasonable continuity and of suitable quality. These are essential factors in marketing Canadian cattle in the British Isles. If it were possible to organize the disorganized farmers so that continuity of supply to the British market might be assured, this would go a long way to solve the problem of the British market and at the same time to ensure that the shipping companies would provide continuous space for the cattle movement. I think the experience of the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Trade and Commerce in 1931, 1932, 1933 and 1934 might be considered in the present circumstances.
That continuity of supply applies to many other commodities.

It does, but this question of the movement of cattle is vital. There is serious distress; in fact, the interjection of the minister tempts me to point out that the price of cattle to the farmers in Canada is not a fair price or one based upon the law of supply and demand at all. It is fixed in Toronto by the heads of the packing institutions, and that condition is unfair to the farmers. I am going to have more to say about that later on. I feel strongly on this question, because next to grain, if not indeed equally with grain, the marketing of live stock is one of the largest items in the production of new wealth in this country. There is no question in my mind-and I have given the matter a great deal of study-that the farmers of Canada are to-day, and have been-I was going to use the word "defrauded"-deprived, and unjustly deprived, of millions of dollars
annually that they should get. I am prepared to prove that, and I shall do so one of these days. I am almost tempted to proceed with an analysis of these conditions, but I did not rise for that purpose to-night. When it is suggested that these conditions apply to other commodities, that is true, but there is nothing in the whole realm of activity in Canada to-day comparable with the unfairness in connection with marketing live stock.

The officials who went to Montreal and other eastern ports at the time mentioned, three or four weeks ago, did review what had taken place along about 1931 and 1932, and had in mind an endeavour to arrange something similar at this time. That could not be done to advantage because of the fact to which I referred a few moments ago. Boats that are going to carry live stock on their decks must carry something else in their holds in order to pay for their passage across the ocean. We found that it was absolutely impossible to do what was done in 1931 if we were to be able to pay the additional cost of doing it. We would have to pay practically the whole cost of a boat going across the ocean and back again, and when we figured that into the costs it was found impossible to obtain anyone who would undertake the work at any price that we could pay. Then, as the Minister of Trade and Commerce says, we could not have obtained sufficient space in any case. There would have been a very small increase in the space that would have been available.
With regard to the last few remarks of the hon. member for Kootenay East, while there may be a great deal of truth in the statement that we are not obtaining enough for our cattle, I think it is pretty well agreed, particularly by those of us who are raising cattle, that there is a feature of the present situation which should be mentioned when we are discussing it from that point of view. Cattle were seventeen cents a pound live weight on the Chicago market at one time last year, and I think one day they were even eighteen cents. Someone says they were nineteen cents. When cattle are nineteen cents a pound in Chicago, no person, either in Ontario or elsewhere, is going to ship cattle to Great Britain.
Did they have cattle to ship at that time?

So many were shipped just prior to the time they were seventeen cents that we went beyond our quota in a month and a half when we had not expected to go beyond it at all this season. At the beginning of June we were thirty thousand behind as coirmared with the year previous, but after the middle of August our quota had been entirely taken up by the shipment of cattle to the United States. The fact of the matter is that beef got so high in the United States that people began to get out of the habit of eating it. When the price of beef rises to nineteen cents a pound in these times, many people cannot eat it. Whether or not that was the whole cause, something did happen in the United States, and beef went down to a very low price. Then for a few months it paid better to ship cattle to Great Britain, and the farmers went into the shipping of cattle to that market. But I am told by those who have been keeping in close touch with the market during the last week or so, that not very many want to ship to Great Britain. They want to ship to Chicago again, because the price is going up. In other words, these two markets, one on each side of the province of Ontario, do have some influence on the price of cattle in Canada.
If we should have an arrangement under which we could land our cattle continuously in the old country, and supply the market over there, we could do very much better than we are able to do by shipping spasmodically, as has been the case in recent years. When we were discussing this question over there two years ago, the main problem in the minds of the British people who were concerned about the matter was where they were going to get their meat supplies. They had no objection to arranging for meat supplies from Canada, but they had to be fairly well assured that they were going to get those supplies somewhere. If they were to undertake to cut down their supplies of meat from the Argentine, they wanted to be absolutely certain that we could send them their supplies every year. From my experience over there, I am quite satisfied that if we should give an undertaking to the old country that we could supply a certain number of cattle every year, the British market would take all the cattle we in Canada could fit for that market. But I think we shall have to be prepared to develop some plan under which they can be fairly well assured that if they get 60,000 head this year, they will get 60.000 head next year and the year following. If we wanted to put it up to 100,000 head, we could do so if we could so arrange matters that we could con-

tinuously supply that market with 100,000 head a year. I do not think, however, we can do that under anything proposed here.

I should like to say just a word at this time with particular reference to the movement of cattle from western Canada into Manitoba. The discussion here to-night has demonstrated clearly the creditable accomplishments of the Department of Agriculture last fall in the handling of cattle from the drought areas of Saskatchewan and Alberta. We regret, of course, that the probable returns for the finished cattle on the feed lots, not only in Ontario and Quebec b it also in Manitoba, may not be as good as one might have hoped, and no doubt some of the people are going to be disappointed.
I should like to make a reference to the pasture field at Carberry. A concentration point was established there, and in that pasture field there are 130,000 acres. It was all fenced by the dominion government; corrals were built; provision was made, as the minister has said, for testing these cattle for tuberculosis as well as for some blood tests in connection with cattle that were exported to the United States. The total cost was in the neighbourhood of $20,000, and some 18,000 head were handled through there. There is a splendid pasture field there, with plenty of water; and, by the way, last fall that field could have handled a considerably larger number than the
18,000	head which were there. So the cost per head was roughly one dollar, which is a very, very reasonable price.
The point I wished to mention more particularly was the attempt to establish auction selling. The accommodation was very good. These corrals were erected,; there were sorting chutes, and so forth. Men employed there sorted these cattle into uniform lots; they were brought into a yard and then sold by auction. These sales were attended by men from all over the country. I think something was started there that is well worth following up. When we look at the heavy shipments of cattle that ordinarily come from western Canada in the fall of the year, loading our stock yards with a burden they can hardly handle, something may be accomplished in the way of securing a proper price for our cattle through auction selling. This concentration pasture for cattle certainly showed that auction selling could be done, and that people would come there to buy cattle. More than that, I was there on one or two occasions, and invariably the live stock commission men were not buying cattle, because they said they were too high. The result was that those

cattle were being purchased by farmers in Manitoba, Ontario and Quebec, and also some from the United States as well. That, in my view, reacts to the credit of the Department of Agriculture in that they were able to organize a scheme whereby full value could be secured, for those cattle. Often we hear that governments cannot do business as satisfactorily as private institutions. This is one illustration where a government has accomplished something very much to its credit.
A few days ago reference was made to horses which had been put in the same pasture fields, after the cattle were moved out. Some people said that many of those horses died, and that some were not in fit condition to move back to the places whence they came. I had occasion to make inquiry about them, and I find that some local people were taking considerable interest in the pasture field. The horses that are in there are put there by the Saskatchewan government, and not by the dominion government at all. A considerable amount of hay was provided for them, in addition to the pasture they could take from under the snow. Unfortunately the snow became deep, and hay had to be fed. As a matter of fact, a number of those horses were up in years, and their teeth were not in good condition. They were not in a condition suitable to stand outside wintering, and to get their own living from under the snow.
However, despite that condition, provision was made to bring those same horses to the corrals, and they were even fed some grain. Therefore, so far as the attention given to the live stock in that pasture field is concerned!, I would say that it has been well cared for. My chief purpose in rising was to point out what really had been accomplished in the pasture field, and to indicate that, so far as my observations are concerned, it reflects creditably on the Department of Agriculture.

I should like to say
a few words regarding this loss on cattle. We have a ten per cent exportable surplus of cattle in Canada, the other ninety per cent being consumed in this country. Our farmers are actually selling cattle at a loss ten times out of twelve, and that applies from 1920 to 1938. Yet here we are voting large grants of millions of dollars to buy feed for cattle which will be sold at a loss. That is what it amounts to. We have all done that, and we are doing it now. Go into the province of Alberta, where they have plenty of feed, and you will find that the farmers will not feed their cattle. They say: " What is the use of using high-priced feed for cattle which will have to be sold at a loss?" They prefer to sell their feed to the drought area because they can get more for their feed in that way than by feeding it to cattle. It pays them better to sell the feed. As a farmer I know perfectly well that as soon as I purchase feed and bring it to the farm, there is a loss.
We talk about railway deficits, and we talk of raising the wages of railway men and civil servants, and of consumers who would eat beef, but they will not pay the price for beef. We raise railway wages and the price of everything except the price of the very thing the farmer has to sell, and I would point out that the greater proportion of the people of this country are farmers. With increased wages the consumers of this country ought to be buying more of the products of the farm. We have a quota for our cattle shipments to the United States, and as we have a ten per cent exportable surplus of cattle, why should we not ship our cattle to Great Britain and have a quota there? The farmers in the western provinces, particularly in the foothills of Alberta, could produce live stock in abundance if they were given any opportunity of producing it at a profit; but we are actually producing it at a loss, and therefore we are submarginal in regard not only to raising grain but to raising cattle as well. You bring cattle down from the west to the east, and find that you have no market for them. The poor people in Wellington county have to use high-priced feed to feed the cattle and then sell them at a lower price than they bought them for.
Hon. gentlemen to my right are always seeking to make the wages of railway men higher, while the farmers' wages are brought down to nothing. We cannot get anything for our cattle. The people who have had

their wages raised to the limit will not buy the stuff, and the result is that the farmers, who are the back-bone of Canada, are suffering. Hon. gentlemen to my right want industry to be prosperous and wages high, but people getting high wages will not buy beef.
There is something wrong with our economic structure and there should be some stabilization or equilibrium or equation whereby those who are the back-bone of this nation should be able to get the living they are entitled to. I am certain the Minister of Agriculture, when he goes over to Great Britain, can find a market for our beef over there. He may say that the boats are not available; but if we have not a steady flow of cattle and beef products going over there, naturally the boats are not going to be available. I guarantee that Alberta alone, if I went through the western foothills, would ship several thousand head of cattle a year to Great Britain.
